name: Amazon SageMaker
oneLiner: End-to-end platform to build, train and deploy machine-learning models.
whatItIs: SageMaker is AWS's managed machine-learning platform, covering the whole lifecycle: prepare data, build and train models on managed compute, tune them, then deploy to real-time or batch endpoints — without provisioning ML infrastructure yourself. It spans notebooks (Studio), built-in algorithms, bring-your-own frameworks (PyTorch/TensorFlow), distributed training, hyperparameter tuning, a model registry, pipelines for MLOps, and hosting. The newer SageMaker also folds in data and analytics tooling. It's the place ML/data-science teams on AWS take a model from experiment to production.

inPractice.narrative: A data scientist pulls training data from S3 into a SageMaker Studio notebook, experiments, then launches a managed training job on GPU instances that spin up, train, and shut down. A tuning job finds good hyperparameters; the best model is registered and deployed to a real-time endpoint that the app calls for predictions. SageMaker Pipelines automates retraining as new data lands. The managed compute exists only while jobs run — you don't keep a GPU cluster idle.

coreConcepts.detail: SageMaker Studio is the IDE for ML — notebooks, experiments and job management in one place, with managed kernels/compute.
You specify data, a container/algorithm and instance type; SageMaker provisions the compute, runs training, saves the model to S3, and tears the compute down — pay only for job time.
Use built-in algorithms, or bring PyTorch/TensorFlow/scikit or a custom container. Distributed training scales across many instances/GPUs.
Automatic Model Tuning searches hyperparameter space with parallel training jobs to find the best-performing configuration.
Deploy to real-time endpoints, serverless inference, asynchronous, or batch transform — matching latency/cost to the use case.
SageMaker Pipelines defines repeatable train/eval/deploy workflows; the Model Registry versions and governs models for production.

whenToUse: End-to-end ML on AWS: build, train, tune, deploy, monitor.
Managed training on GPU/large instances without running clusters.
Productionising models with endpoints, pipelines and a registry (MLOps).
Distributed training and automated hyperparameter tuning at scale.
Teams wanting ML tightly integrated with S3, IAM and the AWS stack.
whenNotToUse: Simple in-database ML on tabular data — Redshift ML / Athena may be enough.
Just calling a pretrained AI API (vision, language) — use Bedrock/AI services.
Tiny one-off experiments where a local notebook is simpler and free.
Teams with no ML needs beyond analytics — it's a specialist platform.

keyFacts.label: Scope
keyFacts.value: Full ML lifecycle: prep, train, tune, deploy, monitor.

keyFacts.label: Compute
keyFacts.value: Managed training jobs on chosen instances (incl. GPU), spun up per job.

keyFacts.label: Inference
keyFacts.value: Real-time, serverless, async, and batch endpoints.

keyFacts.label: MLOps
keyFacts.value: Pipelines + Model Registry for repeatable production.

pricingShape: SageMaker bills for the compute you use across each phase: notebook/Studio instances while running, training jobs per-second for the instances they use (spun up and down automatically), and hosting endpoints for as long as they're deployed. Real-time endpoints are the classic cost trap — they run 24/7 and bill even with no traffic, so serverless/async inference or shutting idle endpoints saves money. Training with Spot instances cuts cost for interruptible jobs. Storage (S3, model artifacts) is separate. Levers: kill idle notebooks/endpoints, use Spot for training, right-size instances.
gotchas: Real-time endpoints bill continuously while deployed — a forgotten endpoint is a common surprise cost; use serverless inference or delete idle ones.
Idle Studio/notebook instances keep billing — shut them down.
GPU instances are expensive; use Spot for training and right-size instance types.
The platform is broad and can feel heavyweight for simple models — match the tool to the need.
MLOps maturity requires discipline (pipelines, registry); ad-hoc usage drifts into unreproducible models.
